claim: Candida albicans is a commensal microorganism of the human host.
source: Candida albicans is a commensal microorganism of the human host (Ghannoum et al., 2010; Nash et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghannoum et al., 2010 and Nash et al., 2017

claim: C. albicans is normally found on mucosal surfaces and on the skin as part of the normal microbial flora.
source: It is normally found on mucosal surfaces and on the skin as part of the normal microbial flora.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about C. albicans colonization

claim: C. albicans is one of the most common human fungal pathogens.
source: It is also one of the most common human fungal pathogens, causing infections that range from superficial infections such as vulvovaginal candidiasis (Sobel, 2007) to life-threatening systemic infections when the immune system is weakened or when there is damage to epithelial barriers (Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sobel, 2007 and Kullberg and Arendrup, 2015

claim: Candida species are responsible for an estimated 750,000 cases of systemic candidiasis annually.
source: Candida species, of which the most prevalent is C. albicans, are responsible for an estimated 750,000 cases of systemic candidiasis annually, with a mortality rate of around 40% (Bongomin et al., 2017; Pfaller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bongomin et al., 2017 and Pfaller et al., 2012

claim: Systemic candidiasis has a mortality rate of around 40%.
source: Candida species, of which the most prevalent is C. albicans, are responsible for an estimated 750,000 cases of systemic candidiasis annually, with a mortality rate of around 40% (Bongomin et al., 2017; Pfaller et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bongomin et al., 2017 and Pfaller et al., 2012

claim: C. albicans requires iron for its survival.
source: Like most organisms, C. albicans requires iron for its survival.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about iron as an essential nutrient

claim: The low solubility of ferric iron (Fe3+) makes iron acquisition challenging in oxidizing environments.
source: The low solubility of ferric iron (Fe3+) makes iron acquisition challenging in oxidizing environments.
evidence: Supported by established chemical knowledge about ferric iron solubility

claim: Many unicellular organisms express ferric reductases (FREs) on their surface.
source: Many unicellular organisms express ferric reductases (FREs) on their surface, which can contribute to iron acquisition by reducing ferric iron to its more soluble ferrous (Fe2+) ion and/or extracting it from iron chelates (Kornitzer, 2009; Kosman, 2003; Philpott, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kornitzer, 2009; Kosman, 2003; Philpott, 2006

claim: The C. albicans genome contains at least 15 genes encoding FRE-like proteins.
source: The C. albicans genome contains at least 15 genes encoding FRE-like proteins, including Fre1/Cfl1 and the major iron reductase Fre10 (Baek et al., 2008; Hammacott et al., 2000; Knight et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baek et al., 2008; Hammacott et al., 2000; Knight et al., 2005

claim: Heme is a molecule that serves as a cellular cofactor almost universally across life.
source: Heme, or Fe-protoporphyrin IX, is a molecule that serves as a cellular cofactor almost universally across life.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about heme function

claim: Environmental heme can be utilized as an alternative iron source by many organisms.
source: As such, it is present in many natural environments, and thus, environmental heme can be utilized as an alternative iron source by many organisms, via a large repertoire of heme acquisition systems (Donegan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Donegan et al., 2019

claim: HRG-1-like heme transporters conserved from C. elegans to mammals can mediate extracellular heme import or intracellular heme transport.
source: In animals, HRG-1-like heme transporters conserved from C. elegans to mammals can mediate extracellular heme import or intracellular heme transport (Rajagopal et al., 2008; Reddi and Hamza, 2016) and the human membrane protein FLVCR2 functions as a heme importer (Duffy et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rajagopal et al., 2008 and Reddi and Hamza, 2016

claim: The human membrane protein FLVCR2 functions as a heme importer.
source: In animals, HRG-1-like heme transporters conserved from C. elegans to mammals can mediate extracellular heme import or intracellular heme transport (Rajagopal et al., 2008; Reddi and Hamza, 2016) and the human membrane protein FLVCR2 functions as a heme importer (Duffy et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2010

claim: The animal host environment restricts the availability of free iron as part of a defense strategy called 'nutritional immunity'.
source: For microorganisms, the animal host environment poses a particular challenge for iron acquisition, as the host restricts the availability of free iron by a variety of active mechanisms as part of a defense strategy called 'nutritional immunity' (Ganz, 2018; Weinberg, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ganz, 2018 and Weinberg, 1975

claim: Hemoglobin heme comprises about two-thirds of the total iron in the host environment.
source: In this environment, hemoglobin heme, comprising about two-thirds of the total iron, is therefore expected to be a particularly attractive iron source, and indeed it is utilized by many bacterial pathogens via several well-studied mechanisms that involve distinct extracellular hemophore families and plasma membrane ABC transporters (Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Contreras et al., 2014; Ganz and Nemeth, 2015; Hood and Skaar, 2012; Huang and Wilks, 2017).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about iron distribution in the body

claim: Hemoglobin heme is utilized by many bacterial pathogens via mechanisms involving extracellular hemophore families and plasma membrane ABC transporters.
source: In this environment, hemoglobin heme, comprising about two-thirds of the total iron, is therefore expected to be a particularly attractive iron source, and indeed it is utilized by many bacterial pathogens via several well-studied mechanisms that involve distinct extracellular hemophore families and plasma membrane ABC transporters (Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Contreras et al., 2014; Ganz and Nemeth, 2015; Hood and Skaar, 2012; Huang and Wilks, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Contreras et al., 2014; Ganz and Nemeth, 2015; Hood and Skaar, 2012; Huang and Wilks, 2017

claim: Schizosaccharomyces pombe uses a membrane heme receptor to internalize heme.
source: Fungi have also evolved different mechanisms to internalize heme, involving a membrane heme receptor in the case of Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Labbé et al., 2020; Mourer et al., 2015) and an endocytosis-based mechanism in the case of Cryptococcus neoformans (Bairwa et al., 2019; Bairwa et al., 2017; Cadieux et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Labbé et al., 2020 and Mourer et al., 2015

claim: Cryptococcus neoformans uses an endocytosis-based mechanism to internalize heme.
source: Fungi have also evolved different mechanisms to internalize heme, involving a membrane heme receptor in the case of Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Labbé et al., 2020; Mourer et al., 2015) and an endocytosis-based mechanism in the case of Cryptococcus neoformans (Bairwa et al., 2019; Bairwa et al., 2017; Cadieux et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bairwa et al., 2019; Bairwa et al., 2017; Cadieux et al., 2013

claim: C. albicans and other Candida spp. express a family of GPI-anchored and soluble extracellular hemophores containing a heme-binding CFEM domain.
source: C. albicans and other Candida spp. express a distinct family of GPI-anchored and soluble extracellular hemophores containing a heme-binding CFEM domain (Roy and Kornitzer, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roy and Kornitzer, 2019

claim: Pga7 is GPI-anchored to the cell membrane.
source: Pga7 and Rbt5 are GPI-anchored to the cell membrane and the cell wall, respectively, while Csa2 is secreted to the medium (Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004

claim: Rbt5 is GPI-anchored to the cell wall.
source: Pga7 and Rbt5 are GPI-anchored to the cell membrane and the cell wall, respectively, while Csa2 is secreted to the medium (Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004

claim: Csa2 is secreted to the medium.
source: Pga7 and Rbt5 are GPI-anchored to the cell membrane and the cell wall, respectively, while Csa2 is secreted to the medium (Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004

claim: Pga7, Rbt5, and Csa2 can extract heme from hemoglobin and transfer it among themselves.
source: These three CFEM proteins are all able to extract heme from hemoglobin and to transfer it among themselves, consistent with a model where heme captured from hemoglobin or other host heme-binding proteins, such as serum albumin, is transferred across the cell wall to the plasma membrane (Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Pinsky et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuznets et al., 2014; Nasser et al., 2016; Pinsky et al., 2020

claim: Heme binding to the CFEM domain involves a unique aspartic acid-mediated heme-iron coordination.
source: Heme binding to the CFEM domain involves a unique aspartic acid-mediated heme-iron coordination that renders the heme-binding redox-sensitive: only ferriheme (Fe3+) binds to the CFEM domain (Nasser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nasser et al., 2016

claim: Only ferriheme (Fe3+) binds to the CFEM domain.
source: Heme binding to the CFEM domain involves a unique aspartic acid-mediated heme-iron coordination that renders the heme-binding redox-sensitive: only ferriheme (Fe3+) binds to the CFEM domain (Nasser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nasser et al., 2016

claim: Heme utilization in C. albicans requires components of the endocytic pathway and the ESCRT system.
source: Heme utilization in C. albicans requires, in addition to the CFEM hemophores, components of the endocytic pathway and the ESCRT system, and vacuolar function (Weissman et al., 2008), suggesting that it involves endocytosis of the heme to the vacuole.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weissman et al., 2008

claim: Heme utilization in C. albicans requires vacuolar function.
source: Heme utilization in C. albicans requires, in addition to the CFEM hemophores, components of the endocytic pathway and the ESCRT system, and vacuolar function (Weissman et al., 2008), suggesting that it involves endocytosis of the heme to the vacuole.
evidence: Supported by citation to Weissman et al., 2008

claim: Heme utilization in C. albicans involves endocytosis of the heme to the vacuole.
source: Heme utilization in C. albicans requires, in addition to the CFEM hemophores, components of the endocytic pathway and the ESCRT system, and vacuolar function (Weissman et al., 2008), suggesting that it involves endocytosis of the heme to the vacuole.
evidence: Supported by inference from the requirement of endocytic pathway and ESCRT system components

claim: GPI-anchored proteins are not known to be subject to ESCRT-mediated endocytosis.
source: However, GPI-anchored proteins are not known to be subject to ESCRT-mediated endocytosis, suggesting the existence of (an) additional transmembrane protein(s) involved in heme internalization.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about GPI-anchored protein trafficking

claim: Additional transmembrane protein(s) are involved in heme internalization in C. albicans.
source: However, GPI-anchored proteins are not known to be subject to ESCRT-mediated endocytosis, suggesting the existence of (an) additional transmembrane protein(s) involved in heme internalization.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that GPI-anchored proteins are not subject to ESCRT-mediated endocytosis but heme uptake requires ESCRT

claim: Frp1 and Frp2 are plasma membrane proteins related to FREs that are essential for heme uptake and utilization in C. albicans.
source: Here, we describe the identification and characterization of Frp1 and Frp2, plasma membrane proteins related to FREs, that are essential for heme uptake and utilization in C. albicans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Many genomes related to C. albicans carry CFEM proteins related to Pga7, Rbt5, and Csa2.
source: Analysis of genomes from species related to C. albicans indicated that many carry CFEM proteins related to Pga7, Rbt5, and Csa2 (Nasser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nasser et al., 2016

claim: Distinct relatives of Rbt5, Pga7, and Csa2 can be identified in almost every genome of Ascomycete clades most closely related to C. albicans.
source: We found that across fungal genomes of the Ascomycete clades most closely related to C. albicans, distinct relatives of Rbt5, Pga7, and Csa2 can be identified in almost every genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows a proximity tree of Rbt5-related proteins from 14 Saccharomycetales genomes).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Meyerozyma (Candida) guilliermondii completely lacks any coding sequence related to CFEM proteins.
source: One exception is Meyerozyma (Candida) guilliermondii, which completely lacks any coding sequence related to these CFEM proteins, unlike equally distant relatives of C. albicans such as Debaryomyces hansenii (Kurtzman and Suzuki, 2010).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis and citation to Kurtzman and Suzuki, 2010

claim: FRP1 and FRP2 presence is best correlated with the presence of Rbt5-related CFEM genes across fungal genomes.
source: Two genes whose presence was best correlated with the presence of Rbt5-related CFEM genes were FRP1and FRP2 (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic profiling analysis described in Materials and methods

claim: C. albicans Frp1 and Frp2 were previously classified as FREs based on their homology to Fre10 and Cfl1.
source: C. albicans Frp1 and Frp2 were previously classified as FREs (Almeida et al., 2009), based on their homology to the main C. albicans FRE Fre10 (Knight and Dancis, 2006), as well as to Cfl1, another C. albicans protein that was experimentally shown to function as an FRE (Hammacott et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2009; Knight and Dancis, 2006; Hammacott et al., 2000

claim: Frp1 and Frp2 cluster separately from most FRE homologs in phylogenetic analysis.
source: However, alignment followed by phylogenetic tree building indicates that Frp1 and Frp2 cluster separately from most FRE homologs, including Fre10 and Cfl1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Frp1 and Frp2 lack an N-terminal domain present in most other FREs.
source: Notably, Frp1 and Frp2 lack an N-terminal domain present in most other FREs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: Frp1 and Frp2 are 36% identical.
source: Frp1 and Frp2 are 36% identical, and out of 13 Saccharomycetales listed in the Candida Gene Order Browser database (cgob3.ucd.ie; Fitzpatrick et al., 2010; Maguire et al., 2013) that have Frp homologs, 12 have an Frp1 ortholog, and 10 have an Frp2 ortholog.
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison and database analysis with citations to Fitzpatrick et al., 2010 and Maguire et al., 2013

claim: FRP1 is adjacent to PGA7 in the C. albicans genome and they share a promoter region.
source: Interestingly, FRP1 and FRP2 are adjacent to two CFEM protein genes in the C. albicans genome, FRP1 to PGA7 and FRP2 to CSA1. In both cases, the adjacent genes are arranged head-to-head and share a promoter region.
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis

claim: FRP2 is adjacent to CSA1 in the C. albicans genome and they share a promoter region.
source: Interestingly, FRP1 and FRP2 are adjacent to two CFEM protein genes in the C. albicans genome, FRP1 to PGA7 and FRP2 to CSA1. In both cases, the adjacent genes are arranged head-to-head and share a promoter region.
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis

claim: The FRP1-PGA7 synteny is conserved in 75% of genomes where they are present.
source: This synteny is conserved across most genomes (75% for FRP1-PGA7 and 70% for FRP2-CSA1; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The FRP2-CSA1 synteny is conserved in 70% of genomes where they are present.
source: This synteny is conserved across most genomes (75% for FRP1-PGA7 and 70% for FRP2-CSA1; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The frp1-/- strain is unable to form colonies on plates with hemoglobin as the sole iron source.
source: As shown in Figure 1A, the frp1-/- strain was unable to form colonies on the plate with hemoglobin as the sole iron source.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Reintegration of a wild-type FRP1 allele completely reverted the growth defect of the frp1-/- strain.
source: Reintegration of a wild-type FRP1 allele completely reverted the growth defect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The frp2-/- strain showed no growth defect on hemoglobin plates at neutral pH.
source: In contrast, the frp2-/- strain showed no growth defect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The frp2-/- strain showed a partial defect in heme-iron utilization on alkaline plates.
source: On the alkaline plates, we found that the frp1-/- strain was still unable to form colonies, whereas the frp2-/- strain showed a partial defect in heme-iron utilization, and reintegration of the FRP2 wild-type allele complemented this growth defect (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: In unbuffered YPD, the frp1-/- mutant is unable to utilize hemoglobin-iron.
source: In unbuffered YPD (pH ~ 6.5), the same picture was seen as on plates, with the frp1-/- mutant unable to utilize hemoglobin-iron and the frp2-/- mutant unaffected (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: In unbuffered YPD, the frp2-/- mutant is unaffected in hemoglobin-iron utilization.
source: In unbuffered YPD (pH ~ 6.5), the same picture was seen as on plates, with the frp1-/- mutant unable to utilize hemoglobin-iron and the frp2-/- mutant unaffected (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: In alkaline YPD, the frp1-/- mutant failed to grow on hemoglobin.
source: In alkaline YPD (pH 8.5), the frp1-/- mutant failed to grow, whereas the frp2-/- mutant exhibited reduced growth, suggesting that this mutant is able to utilize hemoglobin, but at a reduced rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: In alkaline YPD, the frp2-/- mutant exhibited reduced growth on hemoglobin.
source: In alkaline YPD (pH 8.5), the frp1-/- mutant failed to grow, whereas the frp2-/- mutant exhibited reduced growth, suggesting that this mutant is able to utilize hemoglobin, but at a reduced rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The frp2-/- mutant is able to utilize hemoglobin at a reduced rate in alkaline conditions.
source: In alkaline YPD (pH 8.5), the frp1-/- mutant failed to grow, whereas the frp2-/- mutant exhibited reduced growth, suggesting that this mutant is able to utilize hemoglobin, but at a reduced rate (Figure 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the reduced growth phenotype

claim: In all media tested, the frp1-/- mutant was as defective as the pga7-/- mutant in heme utilization.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, in all media the frp1-/- mutant was as defective as the pga7-/- mutant, which is lacking the most essential CFEM protein (Kuznets et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Kuznets et al., 2014

claim: Pga7 is the most essential CFEM protein for heme utilization.
source: As shown in Figure 1C, in all media the frp1-/- mutant was as defective as the pga7-/- mutant, which is lacking the most essential CFEM protein (Kuznets et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuznets et al., 2014

claim: In YPD, both the frp1-/- and pga7-/- strains were unable to grow on hemoglobin.
source: In YPD, both the frp1-/- and pga7-/- strains were unable to grow on hemoglobin, and the rbt5-/- mutant showed an intermediate phenotype, as noted before (Kuznets et al., 2014; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004) whereas on hemin, growth of frp1-/- and pga7-/- was partially restored at higher concentrations, to similar extents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citations to Kuznets et al., 2014 and Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004

claim: On hemin in YPD, growth of frp1-/- and pga7-/- was partially restored at higher concentrations.
source: In YPD, both the frp1-/- and pga7-/- strains were unable to grow on hemoglobin, and the rbt5-/- mutant showed an intermediate phenotype, as noted before (Kuznets et al., 2014; Weissman and Kornitzer, 2004) whereas on hemin, growth of frp1-/- and pga7-/- was partially restored at higher concentrations, to similar extents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: At pH 8.5, all mutants exhibited reduced growth on both hemoglobin and hemin, with frp1-/- and pga7-/- showing the deepest defect.
source: At pH 8.5, all mutants exhibited reduced growth on both hemoglobin and hemin, with frp1-/- and pga7-/- again showing the deepest defect (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The FRP1p-FRP2 construct could complement the frp2-/- but not the frp1-/- mutant.
source: The FRP1p-FRP2 construct could complement the frp2-/- but not the frp1-/- mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), indicating that differential expression is not the reason that Frp2 is inactive in hemoglobin-iron utilization in unbuffered medium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: Differential expression is not the reason that Frp2 is inactive in hemoglobin-iron utilization in unbuffered medium.
source: The FRP1p-FRP2 construct could complement the frp2-/- but not the frp1-/- mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), indicating that differential expression is not the reason that Frp2 is inactive in hemoglobin-iron utilization in unbuffered medium.
evidence: Inferred from the complementation experiment results

claim: The Frp1 and Frp2 proteins are functionally distinct.
source: Rather, this suggests that the Frp1 and Frp2 proteins are functionally distinct.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of FRP2 under FRP1 promoter to complement frp1-/- mutant

claim: In wild-type cells exposed to 10 μM hemin, the HS1 sensor occupancy became nearly maximal.
source: In medium supplemented with 10 μM hemin, in wild-type cells sensor occupancy became nearly maximal, indicating an increase in cytoplasmic hemin concentration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: The increase in HS1 sensor occupancy was much less in the frp1-/- mutant compared to wild-type.
source: The increase in occupancy was much less in the frp1-/- mutant, and lesser still in the frp2-/- and frp1-/- frp2-/- strains, even when exposed to 30 and 50 μM hemin in the medium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Cellular heme concentrations rise with extracellular heme, but the increase in intracellular heme is much reduced in the frp1-/- and frp2-/- strains.
source: Thus, while cellular heme concentrations do rise with extracellular heme, the increase in intracellular heme is much reduced in the frp1-/- and frp2-/- strains, and almost inexistent in the frp1-/- frp2-/- strain.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Frp2 is more important for heme influx into the cytoplasm than Frp1 under alkaline conditions.
source: The reduced increase in sensor occupancy in the frp2-/- mutant exposed to external hemin compared to the frp1-/- mutant suggests that Frp2 is more important for heme influx into the cytoplasm than Frp1 under these conditions, in spite of Frp1 being dominant for heme utilization even at pH 8.5 (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from the sensor occupancy data in Figure 2 and growth data in Figure 1

claim: Ga-PPIX, Mn-PPIX, Co-PPIX, and Zn-PPIX are toxic to C. albicans.
source: We tested toxicity of these two MPPs as well as of Co3+-protoporphyrin IX (Co-PPIX) and Zn2+- protoporphyrin IX (Zn-PPIX) in YPD medium supplemented with 1 mM ferrozine to induce the heme-uptake pathway, and found that all of them are toxic to C. albicans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: In regular YPD medium, the frp1-/- mutant showed increased resistance to all MPPs tested except Ga-PPIX.
source: In regular YPD medium, the frp1-/- mutant showed increased resistance to all of the MPPs tested except Ga-PPIX.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: In regular YPD medium, the frp2-/- mutant showed increased resistance to Zn-PPIX and to a lesser extent to Mn-PPIX.
source: The frp2-/- mutant showed increased resistance to Zn-PPIX and to a lesser extent to Mn-PPIX but not to Co-PPIX or to Ga-PPIX.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: At pH 7.5, the frp2-/- strain but not the frp1-/- strain showed increased resistance to Ga-PPIX.
source: At pH 7.5, the frp2-/- strain but not the frp1-/- strain showed increased resistance to Ga-PPIX.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Frp1 is more important for MPP toxicity in unbuffered medium and Frp2 for toxicity at pH 7.5.
source: In summary, Frp1 and Frp2 were required for full toxicity of at least some of the MPPs in either unbuffered YPD medium (pH ~ 6.5) or in medium buffered to pH 7.5, with Frp1 being more important for toxicity in unbuffered medium and Frp2 for toxicity at pH 7.5.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Pga7 is not involved in the uptake of MPPs.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, no difference could be detected in the sensitivity of pga7-/- vs. PGA7 cells, indicating that Pga7 is not involved in the uptake of these compounds.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Iron starvation induces the ability of C. albicans cells to take up ZnMP.
source: We found that in a wild-type strain, iron starvation induces the ability of the cells to take up ZnMP, and the addition of hemin to the medium efficiently inhibits it, suggesting that ZnMP is taken up by the same pathway as heme (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The addition of hemin to the medium efficiently inhibits ZnMP uptake.
source: We found that in a wild-type strain, iron starvation induces the ability of the cells to take up ZnMP, and the addition of hemin to the medium efficiently inhibits it, suggesting that ZnMP is taken up by the same pathway as heme (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: ZnMP is taken up by the same pathway as heme in C. albicans.
source: We found that in a wild-type strain, iron starvation induces the ability of the cells to take up ZnMP, and the addition of hemin to the medium efficiently inhibits it, suggesting that ZnMP is taken up by the same pathway as heme (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from the iron starvation induction and hemin inhibition of ZnMP uptake

claim: In C. albicans, the ZnMP fluorescent signal remains mainly associated with membrane-like structures.
source: We also noted that unlike in S. pombe and mammalian cells, where the ZnMP fluorescent signal is diffusely cytoplasmic, in C. albicans, the fluorescent signal remains mainly associated with membrane-like structures.
evidence: Supported by microscopy observations

claim: Both SSB1p-FRP1- and SSB1p-FRP2-harboring cells showed a strong intracellular ZnMP signal.
source: Both SSB1p-FRP1- and SSB1p-FRP2-harboring cells showed a strong intracellular ZnMP signal (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Frp1 and Frp2 are each sufficient to mediate uptake of ZnMP.
source: This indicates that Frp1 and Frp2 are each sufficient to mediate uptake of ZnMP.
evidence: Inferred from the ZnMP uptake in cells expressing either SSB1p-FRP1 or SSB1p-FRP2

claim: Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP fusion proteins retained heme uptake activity.
source: These fusion proteins retained heme uptake activity, as evidenced by their ability to support growth on hemoglobin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Both Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP signals became visible after induction by iron starvation.
source: Both the Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP signals became visible after induction by iron starvation and were localized at the cell surface and at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and the GFP signals also accumulated in the vacuole (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP are localized at the cell surface and at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: Both the Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP signals became visible after induction by iron starvation and were localized at the cell surface and at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and the GFP signals also accumulated in the vacuole (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP signals accumulated in the vacuole.
source: Both the Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP signals became visible after induction by iron starvation and were localized at the cell surface and at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and the GFP signals also accumulated in the vacuole (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4A

claim: In the absence of hemin, Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP signals were mostly detected in the vacuole.
source: By microscopic observation, the GFP signal increased with time, and in the absence of hemin, was mostly detected in the vacuole.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: In the presence of hemin, the plasma membrane signal of Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP became much more prominent.
source: In the presence of hemin, the plasma membrane signal became much more prominent (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Frp2-GFP expression appeared higher and more prominently vacuolar compared to Frp1-GFP.
source: In addition, Frp2-GFP expression appeared higher, and more prominently vacuolar, compared to Frp1-GFP.
evidence: Supported by microscopy and Western blot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: A significant increase in cell surface GFP signal was detectable for both Frp1-GFP and Frp2-GFP after 30 min exposure to hemin.
source: A significant increase in cell surface GFP signal was detectable for both proteins after 30 min exposure to hemin (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Expression of Frp1 together with Pga7 promoted better growth of the S. cerevisiae hem1 strain on plates containing hemin.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, expression of Frp1 together with Pga7 promoted better growth of the hem1 strain on plates containing hemin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: In liquid medium, expression of Frp1 together with Pga7 enabled growth of the S. cerevisiae hem1 strain at much lower hemin concentrations than in their absence.
source: In liquid medium, expression of Frp1 together with Pga7 enabled growth of the hem1 strain at much lower hemin concentrations than in their absence, consistent with a more efficient heme uptake in these cells (Figure 5B, 2 days).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of Frp1 alone promoted some growth of the S. cerevisiae hem1 strain over background upon longer incubation.
source: Upon longer incubation, expression of Frp1 alone, but not of Pga7 alone, was found to promote some growth over background as well (Figure 5B, 3 days).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Frp1 by itself can promote heme uptake into the cell, albeit with lower efficiency.
source: This observation indicates that Frp1 by itself can promote heme uptake into the cell, albeit with lower efficiency.
evidence: Inferred from the growth of S. cerevisiae hem1 cells expressing Frp1 alone

claim: Six out of the eight closest structural homologs to Csa2 were C. albicans FREs.
source: Remarkably, beyond the five related CFEM hemophore proteins, six out of the eight closest structural homologs to Csa2 were C. albicans FREs (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison analysis using Alphafold predictions

claim: The regions of homology between CFEM proteins and FREs correspond to the predicted extracellular N-termini of FREs.
source: Alignment of the regions of homology showed that they correspond to the predicted extracellular N-termini of these FREs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by structural alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Six of the eight canonical CFEM cysteine residues are conserved and similarly spaced in the predicted FRE N-termini.
source: Despite the low sequence homology between these proteins and Csa2, six of the eight canonical CFEM cysteine residues, forming three out of the four disulfide bonds in the CFEM structure, are nonetheless conserved and similarly spaced in the predicted FRE N-termini, and indeed are predicted to form disulfide bonds in the predicted structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence and structure analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: Of the 12 FRE homologs that have an extended N-terminal domain, 10 have six cysteines with conserved CFEM alignment.
source: Of the 12 FRE homologs that have an extended N-terminal domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), 10 have six cysteines with conserved CFEM alignment, whereas two have only four of the six cysteines conserved (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: The heme iron-coordinating aspartic acid of CFEM domain is conserved in four FREs and replaced by asparagine in six others.
source: An additional key residue of the CFEM domain, the heme iron-coordinating aspartic acid (Nasser et al., 2016), is conserved in four FREs and is replaced by asparagine in six others.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6 and citation to Nasser et al., 2016

claim: The substrate-binding N-terminal domain of fungal FREs assumes the CFEM fold.
source: Taken together, this analysis suggests that the substrate-binding N-terminal domain of fungal FREs assumes the CFEM fold.
evidence: Inferred from the structural and sequence homology between FRE N-termini and CFEM domains

claim: FRP1 is the highest-induced gene under iron starvation conditions, together with RBT5.
source: Indeed, in some reports, FRP1 is the highest-induced gene under iron starvation conditions, together with the CFEM hemophore gene RBT5 (Lan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lan et al., 2004

claim: FRP1 and FRP2 are highly induced under iron starvation conditions by the Hap43/Cap2-Sfu1 system.
source: FRP1 and FRP2 have been previously identified as genes that are highly induced under iron starvation conditions by the Hap43/Cap2-Sfu1 system, as well as under alkaline conditions by the Rim101 transcription factor (Baek et al., 2008; Bensen et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Lan et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baek et al., 2008; Bensen et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Lan et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2011

claim: FRP1 and FRP2 are induced under alkaline conditions by the Rim101 transcription factor.
source: FRP1 and FRP2 have been previously identified as genes that are highly induced under iron starvation conditions by the Hap43/Cap2-Sfu1 system, as well as under alkaline conditions by the Rim101 transcription factor (Baek et al., 2008; Bensen et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Lan et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baek et al., 2008; Bensen et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2011; Lan et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2011

claim: FRP1 is essential for heme uptake under all conditions tested.
source: The function of these genes was confirmed experimentally: we showed here that FRP1 is essential for heme uptake under all conditions tested, and that FRP2 contributes to heme uptake under alkaline conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: FRP2 contributes to heme uptake under alkaline conditions.
source: The function of these genes was confirmed experimentally: we showed here that FRP1 is essential for heme uptake under all conditions tested, and that FRP2 contributes to heme uptake under alkaline conditions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: A predicted FRE, CnFre2/CNAG_06821, was identified in C. neoformans as being required for optimal growth on hemin.
source: Interestingly, a predicted FRE, CnFre2/CNAG_06821, was identified in the distantly related basidiomycete fungal pathogen C. neoformans, as being required for optimal growth on hemin as well (Saikia et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saikia et al., 2014

claim: CnFre2 is not required for sensitivity to toxic heme analogs.
source: However, unlike Frp1/2, CnFre2 is not required for sensitivity to toxic heme analogs (Saikia et al., 2014), and CnFre2's N-terminal domain lacks the cysteine arrangement found in CFEM proteins and in C. albicans FRE N-terminal domains.
evidence: Supported by citation to Saikia et al., 2014

claim: CnFre2's N-terminal domain lacks the cysteine arrangement found in CFEM proteins and in C. albicans FRE N-terminal domains.
source: However, unlike Frp1/2, CnFre2 is not required for sensitivity to toxic heme analogs (Saikia et al., 2014), and CnFre2's N-terminal domain lacks the cysteine arrangement found in CFEM proteins and in C. albicans FRE N-terminal domains.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis

claim: The redox sensitivity of CFEM heme binding appears to be essential for CFEM hemophore function.
source: This redox sensitivity of binding appears to be essential for the CFEM hemophore function, because mutant proteins carrying a substitution of the iron-coordination Asp with His can efficiently bind ferroheme as well as ferriheme, but these Asp-to-His mutants are completely inactive in vivo (Nasser et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nasser et al., 2016

claim: Frp1 and Frp2 may function as heme reductases that reduce heme bound to extracellular CFEM hemophores to release it.
source: The homology of Frp1/2 to FREs and their role in heme acquisition therefore raise the possibility that they function as heme reductases, and that the Frp1/2 proteins reduce heme bound to the extracellular CFEM hemophores in order to release it.
evidence: Speculated based on FRE homology and redox-sensitive CFEM heme binding

claim: Frp1/2 function in the transport of metal-substituted heme analogs into the cell.
source: These metal-substituted analogs are either not at all redox-active, or much less so compared to heme, indicating that heme reduction cannot be the sole function of Frp1/2. Rather, these observations suggest that Frp1/2 function in the transport of these molecules into the cell as well.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of Frp1/2 to mediate uptake of non-redox-active metal-substituted heme analogs

claim: The location of Frp1/2 in the vacuole and their partial relocalization in the presence of hemin is consistent with a role as heme receptors shuttling between the plasma membrane and the vacuole.
source: The location of Frp1/2 in the vacuole and their partial relocalization in the presence of hemin is consistent with a role of Frp1/2 as heme receptors shuttling between the plasma membrane and the vacuole (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the localization data shown in Figure 4

claim: The Frp-Pga7 complex is evolutionarily related to the main body and the N-terminal domain, respectively, of the FRE protein family.
source: This suggests that the Frp-Pga7 complex is evolutionarily related to the main body and the N-terminal domain, respectively, of the FRE protein family.
evidence: Inferred from the structural and sequence homology analysis

claim: The Frp1/2-CFEM hemophore pathway represents a new paradigm for heme uptake and utilization.
source: The Frp1/2 -CFEM hemophore pathway thus represent a new paradigm for heme uptake and utilization.
evidence: Concluded from the overall findings of the study

claim: Frp1/2 and the CFEM hemophores form a functional complex that evolved from FREs to enable extracellular heme uptake.
source: We conclude that Frp1/2 and the CFEM hemophores form a functional complex that evolved from FREs to enable extracellular heme uptake.
evidence: Concluded from the functional and evolutionary analysis presented in the study
